title: Sawdust
translation: At the prince's palace in Kamakura there was going to be a game of kickball, but it had rained and the ground still wasn't dry. While everyone was discussing what to do, a man called Sasaki sent over a whole cartload of sawdust. They spread it all over the court, and the mud was no longer a problem. Everyone was impressed. "Fancy him having saved all that, just in case."

Someone was telling this story once, and Lord Yoshida said, "Didn't they have any dry sand ready?" I felt rather embarrassed. The sawdust we'd all thought so clever was a cheap, odd thing to use. Whoever is in charge of the grounds is supposed to keep dry sand ready. That's how it has always been done, apparently.
original: {鎌倉|かまくら}の{中書王|ちゆうしよわう}にて{御|おん}{鞠|まり}ありけるに、{雨|あめ}ふりて{後|のち}{未|いま}だ{庭|には}の{乾|かわ}かざりければ、いかがせむと{沙汰|さた}ありけるに、
{佐々木|ささき}{隠岐入道|おきのにふだう}、{鋸|のこぎり}の{屑|くづ}を{車|くるま}に{積|つ}みておほく{奉|たてまつ}りたりければ、{一庭|ひとには}に{敷|し}かれて、{泥土|でいど}のわづらひ{無|な}かりけり。
「とりためけむ{用意|ようい}ありがたし。」と{人|ひと}{感|かん}じあへりけり。
この{事|こと}をある{者|もの}の{語|かた}り{出|い}でたりしに、{吉田中納言|よしだのちゆうなごん}の、「{乾|かわ}き{砂子|すなご}の{用意|ようい}やはなかりける。」とのたまひたりしかば、{恥|はづか}しかりき。
いみじと{思|おも}ひける{鋸|のこぎり}の{屑|くづ}、{賤|いや}しく{異様|ことやう}のことなり。
{庭|には}の{儀|ぎ}を{奉行|ぶぎやう}する{人|ひと}、{乾|かわ}き{砂子|すなご}をまうくるは、{故実|こじつ}なりとぞ。
literal: When there was a kickball game at the Prince of the Central Affairs Ministry's in Kamakura, after it had rained the garden had not yet dried, so there was discussion of what to do;
Sasaki, the lay monk of Oki, loaded sawdust on a cart and presented a great deal of it, so it was spread over the whole garden, and there was no trouble with mud.
'The forethought of having collected it is rare', people admired together.
When someone told this story, the Yoshida Middle Counsellor said, 'Was there no provision of dry sand?', and I was ashamed.
The sawdust that (we) had thought splendid was a lowly and odd thing.
That the person in charge of the garden ceremonies provides dry sand is established precedent, they say.

notes.text: {中書王|ちゆうしよわう}: Chinese-style title for a prince who headed the Ministry of Central Affairs. The 1925 edition identifies him as Prince Munetaka (1242–1274), a son of Emperor Go-Saga, who was sent to Kamakura as shogun.
{鞠|まり}: kemari, the court game of keeping a deerskin ball in the air with the feet, played on a special court. The edition reads {御|おん}.
A warrior of the Sasaki family and former governor of Oki. The 1925 edition names him Masayoshi. {入道|にふだう}: a man who has taken Buddhist vows but goes on living in the world.

notes.quote: とりためけむ用意ありがたし
notes.text: {用意|ようい}: 'forethought, care taken in advance', not just 'ready' as in modern Japanese. けむ: a guess about the past, 'he must have collected it'. ありがたし: 'rare', so 'admirable'.
The 1925 edition identifies him as Fujiwara no Fujifusa. Modern commentaries often leave him unidentified. The text only gives the house name and the rank.

notes.quote: 乾き砂子の用意やはなかりける
notes.text: やは: a rhetorical question, 'was there no…?' The point is that dry sand was the proper thing, and everyone had missed it.
き: past tense for what the writer saw or felt himself. Kenkō was in the room when Yoshida spoke. The 1925 edition explains the embarrassment: he had not known the precedent either.
{故実|こじつ}: established precedent, the old correct way of doing things. Compare section 33, where an old woman remembers a window better than the experts.
